title: The Sound of Everything
subtitle: Jamie Okonkwo spends his working life making the noises you never notice
text: When you watch a film, almost nothing you hear was recorded while it was being shot. Footsteps, a closing door, a coat sleeve brushing against a wall — all of it is added afterwards by a foley artist, working alone in a small studio full of what looks like rubbish. {0} Most of them have been there for years.

Jamie came to the job sideways. He had studied music, expecting to write it, and took a two-week placement at a post-production house only because a friend dropped out. {1} By the end of the fortnight he had stopped thinking about composing altogether.

The work turns out to be less about imitation than about persuasion. A real punch, recorded honestly, sounds like almost nothing at all. {2} Jamie gets the noise he needs from a wet cloth dropped onto a wooden board.
Some sounds are notorious within the trade. Rain is one of them. {3} Fire is worse, because it has to be built out of three or four separate recordings, none of which is actually fire.

The hardest part, Jamie says, is not making a sound but placing it. Every footstep has to land on exactly the same frame as the foot on the screen. {4} A single step half a frame early will not be noticed by anyone, and yet the scene will feel subtly wrong.
It is a strange kind of invisibility. If the work is good, nobody hears it; if it is bad, nobody can hear anything else. {5} That, he says, is the entire job in one sentence.
He still writes music in the evenings, though he no longer expects anybody to listen to it. {6}
sentences: Poured from a watering can onto a plastic sheet, it comes out sounding like applause, or frying, or radio static — anything except weather.
The best compliment he has ever been paid came from a director who said she had not noticed a single sound in the whole film.
Most foley studios are built below ground level to keep out the noise of traffic.
On his very first afternoon he was asked to produce the sound of a horse walking across wet stone.
After a day spent making a room sound like a room, he says, silence is a luxury.
He watches the same few seconds on a loop, forty or fifty times, walking on the spot in a shallow tray of gravel.
Nobody in a cinema would accept that, however, because other films have taught them to expect something far heavier.
Jamie Okonkwo's shelves hold coconut shells, a broken bicycle, forty pairs of shoes and several boxes of dry pasta.
